name: Formats, Examples, and Avatars
title: Formats, Examples, and Avatars
answer: Formats, examples, and avatars are three practical choices a school makes when it personalizes learning with AI. Offering a lesson in several formats widens access, examples drawn from students' own lives make learning meaningful, and the face given to a tutor avatar can quietly shape how much students trust it. The point is to remove barriers and avoid building bias into the tools, not to sort students by a supposed learning style.

sections.body: This idea covers three design decisions that sit around any personalized lesson: how the material is presented, what examples illustrate it, and what the tutor looks like. A lesson can be offered as text, as audio, and as a visual summary so that more students can reach the same content. Examples can be generated to reflect the community, the class's interests, or the cultures students come from, which makes the material feel relevant. The problem it solves is access and connection, since a single format or a distant example can shut some students out. It also warns against a common mistake, which is treating format choice as a learning style that must be matched to each student.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the classroom a teacher might take one lesson and prepare a written version, an audio version read through Microsoft Immersive Reader, and a visual summary, then let students use whichever helps them get to the content. The text does not give separate grade band guidance, so the same approach applies across year groups, with the teacher choosing formats that suit the age of the class. For examples, a teacher can ask AI for illustrations tied to the local community, to what the class is interested in, or to the cultures represented among the students, then check each one before using it. The teacher's own knowledge of the students is what creates real connection, and AI is only there to generate options. When a school sets up a tutor, it can choose a neutral avatar or leave off a human face altogether.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text labels the learning styles point as research backed, citing Pashler et al., 2008, for the finding that teaching to a student's preferred style has not been shown to improve learning. The avatar point is also presented as research backed, with two experiments reported by Anthis and Kyriakidou-Zacharoudiou, 2026, showing that the race, gender, and age of an AI tutor's avatar shaped how much learners trusted it and whether they followed its guidance. Some avatars were rated more credible for reasons unrelated to the quality of the help. The text offers no study for the formats or examples advice, which rests on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits. Format variety is about access and must not be turned into matching students to a supposed learning style, because that idea is not supported. AI generated examples must be checked by the teacher for accuracy and respect, since the model can fall back on stereotypes, and the teacher's own relationship with students remains the source of genuine connection. For avatars, schools configuring tutors should consider neutral avatars or no human face at all, so that biases about credibility are not built into the learning. The decisions about which formats to offer, which examples to keep, and what a tutor should look like stay with the people in the school.
